title: Liver Tests and Approach to Jaundice

steps.tx: Jaundice (yellow discolouration of skin and sclerae from raised bilirubin) becomes visible when serum **bilirubin** crosses about 2.5 to 3 mg/dL, first in the sclerae. Bilirubin comes from haem breakdown, links to albumin, enters hepatocytes, gets conjugated with glucuronic acid, then leaves in bile. Normal total bilirubin is about 0.3 to 1.2 mg/dL.
steps.say: Jaundice is the yellow discolouration of skin and sclerae that comes from raised bilirubin in the blood. It usually can be seen when the bilirubin level reaches about two point five to three milligram per decilitre. The sclerae are first to show the colour change because that tissue contains much elastin. A normal total bilirubin value is about zero point three to one point two milligram per decilitre.

steps.tx: Serum enzymes split the pattern into **hepatocellular** (cell injury) and **cholestatic** (bile flow block) types. Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and aspartate aminotransferase (AST) rise many fold in hepatocellular injury, while alkaline phosphatase (ALP) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) rise more in cholestasis. The ratio of ALP rise to ALT rise helps separate the two groups before imaging.
steps.say: The liver enzymes form two broad patterns that can guide the next steps of evaluation. Alanine and aspartate enzymes rise many fold when liver cells get injured in a hepatocellular pattern. Alkaline phosphatase and gamma glutamyl transferase rise more when bile flow gets blocked in a cholestatic pattern. The ratio of those rises usually can separate the two groups before any imaging test is ordered.

left.title: Hepatocellular pattern
points: ALT and AST rise many fold

steps.tx: The **liver function tests** (panels that gauge injury plus synthesis plus excretion) include albumin, bilirubin, and the prothrombin time expressed as INR (international normalised ratio) as true function markers. Albumin with a half life near 19 to 21 days falls slowly, so it marks chronic change. Aminotransferases mark injury and can be normal in advanced cirrhosis, so function is judged by albumin, bilirubin, and INR together.
steps.say: True liver function is best judged by albumin, bilirubin, and the prothrombin time reported as INR. Albumin has a half life of about nineteen to twenty one days, so it usually changes slowly over time. The liver enzymes only indicate injury and they can be normal even in advanced cirrhosis. A proper assessment therefore should combine albumin, bilirubin, and INR values together.

steps.tx: Jaundice is usually grouped as **prehepatic** (before the liver, as in haemolysis), **hepatic** (in the liver, as in hepatitis), and **posthepatic** (after the liver, as in common bile duct block). Unconjugated bilirubin is water insoluble, rides on albumin, and stays out of urine. Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and appears in urine as urine bilirubin. That urine result therefore splits the workup at the bedside.
steps.say: Jaundice is often grouped as prehepatic, hepatic, or posthepatic depending on the site of the problem. Unconjugated bilirubin is water insoluble and it remains attached to albumin in the blood. Conjugated bilirubin is water soluble and it can be detected in the urine sample. The urine bilirubin result therefore can split the whole workup at the bedside itself.

steps.tx: Jaundice shows first in the sclerae, then in the palate, and later in the skin. **Pruritus** (itching from retained bile salts) with **acholic stools** (pale clay coloured stools) and dark urine points to cholestasis. Fever with right upper quadrant pain in a jaundiced patient raises cholangitis, because Charcot triad is fever, pain, and jaundice. Look also for spider naevi, palmar erythema, splenomegaly, and a palpable gallbladder, and check for a Courvoisier gallbladder that suggests malignant block.
steps.say: Jaundice is noticed first in the sclerae, then in the palate, and only later in the skin. Itching with pale clay coloured stools and dark urine usually suggests blockage of bile flow. Fever with right upper quadrant pain and jaundice should raise the suspicion of cholangitis in such patients. Spider naevi and palmar erythema also can point to chronic liver disease in these patients.

steps.tx: A focused history covers the onset and progress of jaundice, fever, pain, weight loss, drug use, alcohol use, transfusion history, and family history. Examination checks icterus, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, masses, and stigmata of chronic liver disease. The first laboratory set is **fractionated bilirubin** (direct and indirect fractions) with urine bilirubin and urobilinogen, plus a full blood count, reticulocyte count, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and the prothrombin time. Haemolysis is then tested with a blood film, haptoglobin, and a direct antiglobulin test when needed.
steps.say: A focused history should cover the onset, fever, pain, weight loss, drug use, and transfusion history of the patient. Examination must check icterus, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, and stigmata of chronic liver disease carefully. Fractionated bilirubin with urine bilirubin and urobilinogen is the usual first laboratory set in such cases. A high reticulocyte count with low haptoglobin usually can suggest haemolysis and needs a blood film.

steps.tx: **Ultrasound abdomen** (USG, first imaging test) is the usual first imaging test in adult jaundice because it shows duct dilatation, gallstones, liver texture, and spleen size. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) is the best noninvasive map of the bile ducts. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is both the gold standard for biliary obstruction and the route for therapy. Liver biopsy (tissue sample for histology) is the gold standard for staging parenchymal disease when the cause stays unclear.
steps.say: Ultrasound abdomen is the first imaging test in an adult with new jaundice in most practices. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography provides the best noninvasive map of the bile duct anatomy. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography is the gold standard for biliary obstruction and it also allows treatment. Liver biopsy remains the gold standard for staging parenchymal liver disease when the cause is still unclear.

steps.tx: Jaundice care is cause directed and no drug is given for the colour alone. **Gilbert syndrome** (benign reduced glucuronidation from UGT1A1 variation) needs only reassurance after haemolysis is excluded. **Cholestyramine** (a bile acid sequestrant resin) is the first line drug for pruritus, given in sachets through the day. Nutrition, abstinence from alcohol, and avoidance of hepatotoxic drugs help recovery in most cases, with fat soluble vitamins replaced when cholestasis is prolonged.
steps.say: Jaundice care is always directed at the underlying cause of the problem. Gilbert syndrome is benign and it needs only reassurance after haemolysis has been excluded. Cholestyramine is the first line drug for troublesome itching in cholestasis. Fat soluble vitamins should be replaced when bile flow remains blocked for a long period.

steps.tx: Primary biliary cholangitis is treated first with **ursodeoxycholic acid** (UDCA, 13 to 15 mg/kg daily) under the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) guidance. Autoimmune hepatitis responds first to **prednisolone** (40 to 60 milligram daily with slow taper) plus azathioprine. Acute cholangitis needs urgent ERCP drainage within 24 hours, not antibiotics alone. Recent AASLD guidance adds elafibranor and seladelpar for patients with an inadequate response to UDCA.
steps.say: Primary biliary cholangitis is treated first with ursodeoxycholic acid at thirteen to fifteen milligram per kilogram daily. Autoimmune hepatitis is treated first with prednisolone at forty to sixty milligram daily and then a slow taper. Acute cholangitis requires urgent ERCP drainage within twenty four hours of presentation. Recent AASLD guidance also gives elafibranor and seladelpar as options for inadequate response cases.

left.title: Primary biliary cholangitis
points: Add new drugs if response is poor

steps.tx: **Cholestasis** (bile flow blockage) with prolonged duration causes malabsorption of fats, fat soluble vitamin loss, osteoporosis, xanthomas, and coagulopathy from vitamin K deficiency. Jaundice by itself carries no prognosis, because the cause decides the outcome. Common traps are that unconjugated bilirubin stays out of urine, that conjugated bilirubin enters urine, that pruritus points to cholestasis, and that dark urine with pale stools means bile flow block. Jaundice in urine appears before skin change.
steps.say: Prolonged cholestasis can cause fat malabsorption, vitamin loss, osteoporosis, and coagulopathy from vitamin K deficiency. Jaundice by itself has no prognosis because the underlying cause decides the final outcome. Unconjugated bilirubin stays out of urine while conjugated bilirubin enters the urine sample. Pruritus with pale stools usually can point to cholestasis and a bile flow block.

steps.tx: This review pulls together the numbers, drugs, tests, and signs that carry the highest marks in jaundice questions. Retention of the bilirubin cutoffs, the **urine split** (unconjugated stays out while conjugated enters), the first tests, the first line drugs, and the classic signs protects the score. The bilirubin level alone does not fix the cause, and the urine result decides the next step.
steps.say: This material is built around numbers, drugs, tests, and signs that are most often asked in examinations. Retention of the bilirubin cutoffs and the urine split can protect the score in viva rounds. The first line drug doses and the classic signs are expected to be recalled without delay. A clear grasp of the first tests should prevent many common diagnostic errors.
